A lot of early-stage SaaS companies won’t lose because the product is bad.

Post occasionally. Run ads. Hope something sticks.

That compounds.

I’ve noticed something else too.

Before people buy from a SaaS company now, they often check the founder first.

Their posts. Their thinking. Their consistency.

People want signals before they trust products.

I think the founders who figure this out early will have a huge advantage over the next few years.

Not because they tweet more.

Because they stay visible long enough for trust to build around the product.

Paid ads still work.

But rented attention gets expensive fast.

Owned distribution compounds differently.

Stay creative ✍

text:
Distribution Is the Hard Part

Most founders think the hard part is writing code. It isn’t.
The hard part is getting anyone to care.

You can ship a flawless product, timed perfectly, solving a real problem—and still watch it die in silence. Why? Because no one saw it.

A product without distribution is a secret. And secrets don’t scale.

Founders love to talk about product/market fit but skip the middle step: attention. Real users must discover you, try you, tell a friend, return, repeat. That doesn’t happen on autopilot. It happens because someone—usually the founder—pushes the story into the world.

Hiding behind great code is a bet on luck. Luck isn’t a strategy.

“Focus on the problem” and “build something people want” are half the job. The other half is relentless distribution—transferring your conviction to the market until it spreads on its own.

Build well, yes. But spend just as much energy making people care. That’s how a product becomes real.

text:
Distribution Is the Hard Part

Most founders think the hard part is building the product. It’s not.

The hard part is getting anyone to care.

You can build something great. It can solve a real problem. It can even be timed perfectly. But if no one notices, it dies.

This is where most founders get stuck. They think the job is to build. They think if they make something good enough, growth will take care of itself. That’s rarely how it works.

A product without distribution is like a secret. And most secrets never get out.

When founders talk about product/market fit, they often forget the middle part. The part where people actually have to find the thing. Try it. Tell someone else. Come back. And not just because the product is useful, but because they believe in it.

The truth is, most products don’t spread on their own. People spread them.

That means someone has to push. Someone has to tell the story in a way that makes other people want to be part of it. And that someone is usually the founder.

This is what founders don’t want to hear. That they can’t hide behind the product. That being technical or visionary or obsessed with design isn’t enough. That the work doesn’t stop when the code is deployed.

If you’re not doing the work to get attention, you’re betting on luck. And luck is not a strategy.

People say things like “focus on the problem” or “build something people want.” That’s good advice. But it’s not the whole picture. Because no matter how perfect your solution is, it won’t matter if people don’t know it exists.

Distribution is not a phase. It’s not a channel. It’s not a growth hack.

Distribution is belief. It’s the transfer of energy from the founder to the market. The best founders do it relentlessly. They don’t wait to be discovered. They create momentum.

The best ones know: the product is important, but getting people to care is what makes it real.

Most founders ask:

“How do I get customers?”

But the better question is:

“Where are customers already looking for a solution?”

Because the easiest customers to get are the ones already searching.

Here's my simple framework:

Step 1: answer questions

Your content should answer the questions customers already ask.

People search:

“How to reduce churn”

These searches are all active demand.

Step 2: Create a solution page.

Content:

- Explain the problem
- Show a simple method
- Offer a free workout plan

This page becomes a lead generator.

Step 3: Offer a deeper resource

This literally works in every industry.

Examples:

Plumber
→ “Home Plumbing Emergency Checklist”

Gym owner
→ “7-Day Beginner Fat Loss Plan”

Consultant
→ “Client Acquisition Scripts”

SaaS founder
→ “Startup Pricing Calculator”

People can download it by entering their email.

Step 4: Follow up automatically

Send 3–5 automated emails.

Email 1: Deliver the calculator
Email 2: Explain the biggest retention mistake
Email 3: Show a real SaaS churn example
Email 4: Teach a quick tactic
Email 5: Offer your product

Now people move from:

search → lead → customer automatically.

text:
Most people use ChatGPT wrong.

They ask questions like "How do I get customers?" then wonder why they get a generic 5-step framework that looks identical to the first search result on Google.

The real power of AI isn't simply getting quick answers (like from a Google search) — it's in getting personalized insights that directly address your unique situation.

For example, last month, we opened up our beta to more users.

Instead of simply prompting ChatGPT for “how to get more signups for our beta product”, I wrote something a bit more specific (here’s a real excerpt from a Deep Research prompt):

"Research the most prominent leaders in growth marketing (startup founders and people who lead/led growth for early-stage startups). Make sure to include @ElenaVerna, Brian Balfour, @Julian, @gauravvohra, @Lennysan, and others. Then create a guide based on their advice and best practices. Consider the state of our product, team, business model and ask me any questions needed to fill in the gaps: [Workmate’s current context]... Then include a step-by-step for what we should do over the coming 3 months…"

ChatGPT didn't just spit out generic advice — it asked follow-up questions to understand our situation better, like which growth frameworks I prefer and what specific challenges are most top-of-mind.

The result?

A customized strategy incorporating best practices from some of my favorite growth leaders, all tailored to our specific goals and constraints.

The difference is subtle but powerful: I wasn't asking AI to do my thinking for me — I was making it my thinking partner.

text:
Tonight, @SuperteamMY co-hosted a session with @ryantjhin_ and had @mattytay in da house 🏛️

@colosseum co-founder, spilling how to actually win Colosseum

here's what the G said 👇

(if you're in Colosseum and skip this… I don't know why you're still participating. no point, you will lose)

1/ it's not a hackathon. it's a startup competition.
no bounties. no weekend side projects. they want the top 0.1% of builders willing to quit their jobs.

bring an existing project, pivot mid-way, or start fresh. evolving an idea across hackathons = encouraged. resubmitting the same thing unchanged = not.

2/ the pitch video gets watched FIRST

2 min hard limit. judges want to know who you are before anything else.

cover:
→ who you are + why you're building this
→ the insight you found
→ product, user, early demand
→ what you built + why those features
→ the big vision

technical deep-dive goes in the demo video. get on camera. AI narration is fine if English isn't your first language.

3/ what judges actually look for

→ deep domain knowledge + a non-obvious insight
→ a novel angle (don't just clone Polymarket)
→ ideas that failed before but work NOW
→ obsession + commitment
→ real retention > incentive-farmed users

the big filter: can this be venture-scale?
a great restaurant is a good business. it's not a startup.

4/ the #1 thing founders forget: your first users

"we'll tweet about it" is not a plan.
best products have growth built in, like Axiom's referrals or FOMO's social features.

5/ after you submit, KEEP BUILDING

first interview question is often "what have you done since the hackathon?"

thousands of submissions → a few hundred deep reviews → ~150–200 interviews → stack-ranked for winners + investment

6/ quick facts

→ open to all chains, but the accelerator stays mostly Solana
→ $250K standard deal, ~10 teams per cohort
→ solo founders OK, co-founders preferred (there's a matching tool)
→ non-technical OK if you're good with AI coding tools
→ tokens aren't a dealbreaker, but they're a one-way door
→ university + public goods awards open to all chains

save this. read it before you submit.

And then… what?

There’s no universal roadmap for getting the first users because every product has a different audience, stage, channel and story.

Since then, I’ve been rebuilding BuildTraction around that problem.

I’d love to work closely with a few founders for free before I put up the paywall and properly launch it.

text:
One thing I’m learning building @POVMarket is that a trading platform has a cold start problem that looks a lot like a social app.

People join a social app because other people are there. Which is a difficult thing to offer when you’ve just started.

With trading, people want to be where other people are trading. They want activity, liquidity, something happening. But those are all things that become easier to provide once people have already shown up.

You’re asking the first users to join something that gets better with the users who come after them.

I think a lot of CT is fairly open to what they trade. NFTs one day, meme coins the next. Could be onchain stamp collections for all we know. I’d like opinion markets to be next. Making that happen is my job.

Of course, these assets are different. But I don’t think people move between them because they’ve carefully concluded that one is fundamentally better than another.

NFTs didn’t stop being collectible. What changed was how many people wanted to collect them, trade them and talk about them. A big part of the experience was everyone else being there.

That matters when you’re trying to figure out what to build next.

When activity is low, there’s always another feature you could add. We have plenty of ideas at POV. Some are good, and we’ll build them. But I keep asking myself: would this make someone want to trade, or would it mostly make things nicer for someone who already wanted to?

Those are both useful. They solve different problems.

At this point, I think POV is a great product. I’m also the founder, so saying that is the easy part. We still have to get people to show up, come back and bring someone with them.

My current belief is that getting that loop going matters more than finding some new mechanic that supposedly makes the whole thing go viral.

Polymarket launched in 2020. Its 2024 election breakout came years later. There was a lot of work between those two points, and an election gave people a very specific reason to use it. But the core idea had to survive long enough to get there.

I think there’s a cost to constantly changing a product that’s easy to miss.

Your first users have to understand it. Then they have to like it enough to explain it to someone else. That person might take a while to try it. If you change the idea halfway through, the thing their friend liked may no longer be the thing they find.

You can keep restarting the process before it has a chance to go anywhere.

That doesn’t mean you ignore feedback or stick with something regardless of the evidence. But you need a core idea you believe in, and some patience with how long it takes other people to see what you see.

For POV, I want us to keep making the product better, while putting most of our effort into getting people through the door and giving them a reason to stay.

More people trading together. More conversations around the markets. More people sending a link to a friend because something interesting is happening.

We haven’t earned that momentum yet. That’s the work in front of us.

Am I the only one seeing this?

text:
HOW TO FIND WHAT WEB3 BUILDERS ARE BUILDING BEFORE LAUNCH (worth reading) 😳

most people find a project when the website is already live, the community is active and ct is talking about it.

at that point, you’re usually late.

if you want to find projects early, stop searching for “upcoming projects”.

find the people building them.

here’s how i’d actually do it:

START WITH GITHUB

search for repos around the narratives you’re interested in.

don’t just look at the repo name.

check when it was created, recent commits, contributors, issues and how often the code is changing.

a repo with 2 commits from 8 months ago means nothing.

a small repo getting regular commits from multiple people is much more interesting.

FIND THE BUILDERS BEHIND IT

once you find an interesting repo, check the contributors.

look at their github profiles.

then find their x accounts.

now check what they’re talking about, who they interact with and what other builders they follow.

one good developer can lead you to an entire network of people building in the same space.

WATCH THE CONVERSATION BEFORE THE ANNOUNCEMENT

this is where it gets interesting.

a builder might start talking about a problem months before launching anything.

first it’s a random technical post.

then a discussion.

then a prototype.

then someone asks for testers.

then a github repo appears.

then suddenly there’s a “stealth” project.

don’t wait for the final announcement.

watch the progression.

LOOK AT WHO IS WORKING WITH WHO

if you find one serious builder, check their replies and interactions.

who keeps showing up?

which developers are collaborating?

which researchers are discussing the same problem?

which accounts suddenly start interacting with each other?

you’re basically mapping the people around a project before the project becomes obvious.

CHECK TESTNETS AND ACTIVITY INSIDE IT

sometimes the first signal isn’t on x at all.

look for new contracts, testnet deployments, documentation, wallets interacting with new protocols and early transactions.

use explorers, dune, defillama and other onchain tools to verify what you’re seeing.

a random “big things coming” tweet is easy to fake.

actual activity is harder to fake.

WATCH FOR PEOPLE HIRING

this is one of the easiest signals to miss.

if a team suddenly needs smart contract engineers, protocol researchers, frontend developers, devrel or growth people, something is usually happening behind the scenes.

read the job description carefully.

you can often figure out what they’re building from the skills they’re looking for.

FOLLOW THE INFRASTRUCTURE

you don’t always discover a project from the project itself.

sometimes you discover it through the companies building around it.

an oracle integration.
a wallet integration.
a bridge.
an analytics dashboard.
an audit.
a grant.
a developer tool.

these can reveal what’s coming before the main project starts marketing itself.

BUILD YOUR OWN WATCHLIST

don’t just bookmark random posts.

make a simple list of projects you’re watching.

track:

founder
builders
github
X Account
narrative
testnet
last activity
what changed
potential opportunities

then check it every few days.

being early can mean being one of the first users, testers, contributors, community members or people who actually understand the product.

and obviously, do your own research.

end of the day, the goal is to build a system where you can consistently find interesting builders before the rest of ct notices them.

bookmark it ASAP

text:
if you have an app idea, don’t open Lovable, Bolt or Cursor yet.

open your notes first.

after working on 20+ products, these are the 10 things I want written down before we start building:

what are we building?

explain the app in one or two paragraphs. what does it help people do?

who is it for?

not “everyone.”

who has the problem, and how are they currently dealing with it?

what already exists?

check similar apps.

read their reviews too. people will literally tell you what they like, what they hate and what they wish the app could do.

what must the first version do?

make a list of the features people genuinely need.

everything else can wait.

how will someone use it?

map what happens from the moment they open the app until they get the main result.

include signup, payment and the boring parts too.

what will the screens look like?

rough wireframes are fine.

boxes, buttons and ugly sketches are enough at this stage.

how should each feature behave?

“add subscriptions” isn’t enough.

what are the plans? is there a trial? what happens when payment fails or someone cancels?

what should the app feel like?

save references for the colours, type, layout and general design direction you want.

what does it need to connect to?

payments, AI models, notifications, maps, live data, third-party APIs, write all of it down.

how will people find it?

don’t wait until launch to start thinking about marketing.

decide where the first users will come from and what will tell you they actually find the app useful.

none of this needs to look fancy.

your product brief can be one page.

your user flow can be boxes and arrows.

your wireframes can be ugly.

the point is to answer the confusing questions before they become expensive changes halfway through development.

AI can turn a prompt into screens in minutes.

if these things aren’t clear, you’ll spend the rest of the project changing those screens.

this is part of my AI App Development Playbook.

save it for your next app idea.

text:
Why was it delisted?

$REP (Reputation/Augur)

Augur was supposed to be the most ambitious prediction market ever built on Ethereum. It raised $5.3 million in 2015 and promised to replace all centralized betting with decentralized, trustless prediction markets. The Reputation token was the backbone, helping resolve predictions and incentivizing honest behavior.

It worked on paper. In practice, it was a nightmare.

The resolution mechanism was so complex that watching an Augur market resolve felt like watching paint dry through a legal document. Fees were brutal. UX was painful. By 2019, the platform had basically given up on its own vision and became a ghost town of abandoned markets worth fractions of a cent.

Then in 2021, Augur v2 launched and nobody showed up. Transaction costs on Ethereum had exploded, resolving markets cost hundreds of dollars, and traders had moved to Polymarket years earlier.

In 2024, Augur shut down operations entirely. REP got delisted from major exchanges not because of fraud or a hack, but because the product stopped existing and $REP became worthless. Sometimes the best idea at the worst time just dies slowly instead of crashing fast.

It proved prediction markets worked as a concept, just not that way, on that chain, at that cost.

text:
If you want to build a system that gets you leads EVERY SINGLE DAY, as in no day goes by without someone coming to ask about whatever it is you sell, I'm going to share a 2 things I have never shared before on how to actually hack that.

1. Find the exact moment people realize they need what you sell, then show up there.

For example, if you teach people how to sell digital products, don't only create content around "how to make more sales."

Think about what happens five minutes before someone realizes they need help selling.

Maybe they just launched and nobody bought, Maybe someone asked for their price and disappeared.

Those are trigger moments.

Now create content around those exact situations.

When someone experiences that problem, your post should feel like you somehow knew what just happened to them.

That person is far more likely to come to you because they aren't randomly seeing your offer. They're seeing you at the exact moment their need becomes urgent.

2. Create content people can accidentally send you leads with.

This one is my favourite.

You know when you see a post and immediately think, "Omo, this is exactly what Tolu needs to see"?

Create more of those.

Don't only write content for the person who needs your product.

Write some content so clearly around a person's problem that someone else can identify that person and send the post to them.

For example:

"Send this to that friend of yours who has been creating digital products and complaining that nobody is buying."

Now your audience becomes part of your distribution.
